claim: Different load measures disagree: single-item ratings and eye measures detect and match intrinsic-load manipulations best; brain measures match worst (EEG beta 0% match). Detection: subjective 94%, eyes 87%, skin 85%, heart 68%, brain 68%; match with expected ordering: 78/78/62/64/32%. Vote counts over 28 studies, not effect sizes. (Re-checked against the paper text.)
agent_test: Do not trust one proxy. Log several cheap proxies (output tokens, self-rated difficulty, answer stability across samples) on the same items and check which track a known difficulty ordering.
audit_note: Ayres et al. 2021 tables verified (detection 94/87/85/68/68%, match 78/78/62/64/32%, EEG beta 71%/0%, 28 studies, 33 experiments); Scheiter et al. 2020 exists and supports measure disagreement qualitatively.

claim: Subjective ratings of the three load types (intrinsic, extraneous, germane) are reliable (pooled alpha .73 to .85) but do not separate cleanly: ICL and ECL correlate positively (r+=.298, k=25) and ratings relate only weakly to learning (r about .1 to .26). Germane ratings are the weakest.
agent_test: Warns against an agent-side three-score load rating step. Test a one-number difficulty rating against accuracy instead.
audit_note: Krieglstein et al. 2022 text supports alphas .734-.851, positive ICL-ECL correlation, weak correlations of ratings with learning and weak germane ratings; the specific r+=.298 (k=25) and the .1-.26 range sit in tables that could not be text-checked (range may be ~.06-.26).

claim: Germane load is not a separable, measurable construct: a two-factor model (intrinsic plus extraneous) fits well, and germane items are the weakest in several validations. Klepsch 2017 still argues for three.
agent_test: Keep only two budget lines in the scaffold (task difficulty, clutter). Add a germane knob only if it beats two knobs at equal tokens.

claim: Single-item mental-effort/difficulty ratings (including the 9-point Paas scale) did best in the physiological comparison (Ayres 2021), and in a questionnaire meta-analysis odd-point scales (5 or 9) were more reliable than even-point ones for extraneous load, though 10-point scales scored highest for intrinsic load and 11-point for germane load; which scale format tracks performance best depends on task complexity (numeric scales for complex problems, pictorial for simple ones; Ouwehand 2021).
agent_test: If the agent self-rates difficulty, use a 9-point scale and test its rank correlation with correctness on held-out items.
audit_note: Krieglstein reports odd scales (5 or 9 points) more reliable than even ones for ECL, but 10-point best for ICL and 11-point best for GCL, and it concerns multi-item questionnaires, not the single-item scale; Ayres supports single items doing best physiologically; Ouwehand supports the task-complexity dependence.
claim_before_audit: The 9-point single-item mental-effort or difficulty scale is the best-supported rating format (odd-point and 9-point scales most reliable; single items did best in the physiological comparison). Which scale tracks performance best depends on task complexity.

claim: Raw (unweighted) NASA-TLX is not safe as a stand-in for weighted TLX: in one small online study the weighted score was 65.29 versus 51.81 raw in the long arm (n=7).
agent_test: Not applicable to the agent (no pairwise weighting by a person). Low priority.

claim: Self-rated effort behaves like a metacognitive cue rather than a direct readout of load: perceived effort is negatively related to monitoring judgments (beta=-.19) and has a small negative indirect link to learning via monitoring (beta=-.05) with a non-significant direct link (beta=-.07, CI -.16 to .02; model saturated, interpret with caution); Scheiter et al. 2020 review evidence that people use heuristic cues when appraising effort and suggest response time as a candidate objective effort measure.
agent_test: The agent's own confidence ratings will be cue-based too. Compare agent self-confidence with a behavioural check (agreement across resamples) before using it to gate extra work.
audit_note: David et al. 2024 numbers verified (indirect beta=-.05, direct -.07 ns, 35 papers/83 samples) but the direct estimate is numerically larger, the authors flag the saturated model as to-be-interpreted-with-caution, so 'mostly through confidence judgments' is too strong; Scheiter et al. say people use heuristic cues for effort appraisals, with response time being how effort-as-a-cue is operationalised in metacognition work, not a shown cue for effort ratings.
claim_before_audit: Self-rated effort is a metacognitive cue, not a direct readout of load: effort affects learning mostly through confidence judgments (indirect beta=-.05; direct beta=-.07, ns), and raters use heuristic cues such as response time.

claim: Dual-task measures are fragile: the modality effect appeared in secondary-task reaction times only with a spatially non-contiguous secondary task (partial eta2=.17) and vanished with a contiguous one (F=0.03). Design choices create or hide effects and the field lacks standardisation.
agent_test: The analogue is a probe task during reasoning; likely not worth it. Prefer free measures already in the output (token counts).
audit_note: Schoor et al. abstract verifies the modality effect only with the spatially non-contiguous secondary task and N=96 (46/50); the partial eta2=.17 and F=0.03 are paywalled and unchecked (F(1,94)=20.17 would give about .18); Esmaeili Bijarsari verifies lack of standardisation of dual-task paradigms.

claim: Load measures do not transfer across task types: validity varies by task class (memory tasks 90% match, arithmetic 65%, heart measures on word tasks 0%).
agent_test: Calibrate any load proxy per task family on the agent, never globally.
audit_note: Ayres Table 6 verified memory 90% match, arithmetic 65% match, heart on word tasks 0%, though the word-task heart cell is only 2 experiments and 'do not transfer' is the claim's inference from varying vote rates.

claim: LLM reasoning-token counts track human response time (within-task rho .24 to .91 for GPT-OSS; DeepSeek-R1 mean rho .57; content moderation, six models: overall r=.15 to .19, humans 26 to 39 percent slower in the top vs bottom CoT-length quintile). Token count is a usable but weak item-level proxy for cognitive cost. Update: within the same item, longer chains also go with LOWER accuracy (d05, d06), so tokens carry error information as well as time.
agent_test: Use output tokens per item as the load proxy. Correlate tokens with error rate on a mixed-difficulty set at equal total budget and check it beats self-rated difficulty.
audit_note: Davidson (six models, r=.15-.19, 26-39% slower top vs bottom quintile), Hu & Wang (r .24-.91 across GPT-OSS tasks, .57 de Varda DeepSeek-R1 mean), Feng (question-fixed-effect negative length) and Ballon (-3.16/-1.96/-0.81 per 1000 tokens) verified; slips: those are Pearson r not rho, and Ballon controls for difficulty tier and domain rather than being strictly within the same item.

claim: The reasoning-effort setting acts as a cap, not a dial: GPT-OSS effort low/medium/high changed token length but not alignment with human RT (mean .570/.567/.562; BF10 about .4, inconclusive). Vankov et al. (second-hand) report negligible accuracy effect of effort in 5 of 6 tasks.
agent_test: Measure accuracy against token budget on our items before adding any 'think longer' operator.

claim: Accuracy falls as load sources rise in LLMs, with task length the strongest knob: CogniLoad on 22 models (N=20 to 50: DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66; Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40; by d=5 12 of 22 below 50%; at N=250 only gpt-5 .76 and o3 .68 above .50). Intrinsic d and log N are negative in every model. ECL50 gpt-5 382.8, o3 356.9 re-checked.
agent_test: Files a and c cover the same paper, so this is one source. Decompose a task into fixed-size subtasks and compare with one long chain at equal tokens.

claim: Irrelevant context lowers LLM accuracy on some benchmarks: GSM-IC (under 30% of base problems solved under all distractor variants for 2022-era models) and ICE (Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.85 control to 0.72 at 80% junk, slope -0.003 per percent; a length-matched control at 0.82 was not significantly different from control, p=.45, one model, small independent preprint). CogniLoad finds a U-shaped, not monotone, response to distractor ratio and names task length as the dominant stressor, so length is not ruled out as a factor.
agent_test: Add an 'ignore irrelevant information' line plus a context filter. Test accuracy at equal tokens on a distractor-augmented set.
audit_note: GSM-IC (<30% macro) and ICE numbers (Gemini 0.85 to 0.72, slope -0.003, long control 0.82 p=.45) verified, but ICE shows a significant effect only for Gemini (GPT-4o slope ns, three models at 0%), 'length alone' rests on a non-significant p for one model, and CogniLoad reports task length as a dominant stressor and a U-shaped (non-monotone) distractor response, so it does not support a simple 'irrelevant context lowers accuracy, length does not explain it'.
claim_before_audit: Irrelevant context lowers LLM accuracy: GSM-IC (under 30% of base problems solved under all distractor variants for 2022-era models), ICE (Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.85 control to 0.72 at 80% junk, slope -0.003 per percent; length-matched control 0.82, p=.45), CogniLoad. Length alone does not explain it.

claim: Distractor effects on LLMs are non-monotonic and model-specific: CogniLoad shows lowest accuracy at 25 to 50 percent needle with recovery at the extremes for most models (quadratic term better AIC in 18 of 22), and the opposite direction in a few. A linear load score would mislead.
agent_test: Probe the agent at three distractor ratios, not two, before fitting any linear load model.

claim: Prompt-side remedies cut distraction at no cost on clean tasks: an explicit 'feel free to ignore irrelevant information' line, distractor exemplars, and self-consistency (about +11 points micro on average, +35.5 points on 0-CoT; best macro accuracy still only 45%). Old models only. Update (2026, DNR Bench, 1000-token cap): an instruction line raised accuracy a lot for DeepSeek-R1 (redundant .00 to .76) and Claude-3.7-Thinking (.40 to 1.00) but not for o3-mini-high (.00 to .04), and hurt on the 'indifferent' category (Claude .80 to .04). Model specific, can backfire.
agent_test: Ablate one ignore-line instruction on a distractor set at equal tokens and check clean accuracy holds (source: GSM8K CoT 59.3 vs 60.3).

claim: Small or weak models fail at baseline, so extraneous-load effects cannot be read (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B and Mistral-7B 0% in every ICE condition; CogniLoad low-capacity models). Load manipulations need a baseline the model can already solve.
agent_test: Use item sets where the agent's clean accuracy is 30 to 90 percent before testing any load effect.
audit_note: Adapala ICE verified (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, Mistral-7B 0% EM across all conditions incl. control); CogniLoad capacity thresholds near 0 for the smallest models verified from abstract-level and listed figures; 'baseline must be solvable' is the claim's inference.

claim: Load-aware prompting that cuts tokens at near-equal accuracy is reported (CLAI-Prompt: GSM8K 92.5 to 92.3 at 485 to 310 tokens; MATH 53.9 to 53.5) but only in one unreplicated single-author preprint with no variance, a baseline mismatch between tables (GSM8K CoT 92.5 vs 90.1), and a Llama-3-8B student at 90.1 on GSM8K that looks high.
agent_test: Compare a short-budget plan-then-solve prompt with plain CoT on accuracy per token on our items. Treat the 35 percent saving as unverified.

claim: CLT-inspired multi-agent decomposition helps on high-intrinsic-load reasoning tasks (LiveBench Math 75.3 vs 70.0) but hurts instruction-following (81.8 vs 84.4), at about 20 times the tokens (13.5k to 14.3k vs 650 to 710 per question). Contested: at equal thinking-token budgets a single agent matched or beat five multi-agent designs on multi-hop QA (Tran and Kiela 2026).
agent_test: a20 and c23-c25 are the same arXiv paper (2506.06843). Test split-into-specialists against single pass at EQUAL tokens; the source does not.

claim: Structure helps more when the token budget is tight (8,192-token cap: Gemini-2.5 Reasoning 69.2 vs 31.0 plain). Tran and Kiela find multi-agent gains shrink once thinking tokens are matched and flag API budget-control artifacts, so a tight-cap advantage may be a budget artifact.
agent_test: Rerun a structured vs plain comparison at several token caps and plot the gap.

claim: Models spend large token budgets on easy problems (overthinking) and reasoning effort rises then falls with complexity before accuracy collapses, so token spend is not a monotone load indicator. Abstract-page evidence only.
agent_test: Cap tokens by estimated difficulty and measure the accuracy loss on easy items; verify against full texts first.
audit_note: Abstracts of Chen 2024 (overthinking on simple problems), Shojaee 2025 (effort rises then declines with complexity, accuracy collapse), Su 2025 and Singh et al. verified; Shojaee's puzzle findings are contested elsewhere but match their abstract.

claim: Multi-turn and long-context position effects degrade LLM performance (39 percent average drop over 200k simulated conversations; lost in the middle). They are cheap load manipulations but not CLT measures. Abstract-page evidence only.
agent_test: Restate the task in one clean message rather than relying on a long dialogue; test at equal tokens.
audit_note: Laban et al. abstract (39% average drop, 200,000+ simulated conversations, six tasks) and Liu et al. lost-in-the-middle verified; the 'cheap load manipulations but not CLT measures' part is the author's judgement.

claim: Perceived task difficulty and mental effort are distinct constructs: effort vs perceived difficulty r=.78; difficulty tracks relative item difficulty more tightly for open-ended items (r=-.80) than multiple choice (r=-.45).
agent_test: Log an effort proxy (tokens) and a difficulty proxy (answer disagreement across samples) separately.
audit_note: Schuessler et al. 2024 verified (effort vs perceived difficulty r=.78; -.80 open-ended n=65 vs -.45 multiple choice n=61); the paper itself says .78 supports that the two ratings differ, 'distinct constructs' is a slightly strong gloss for a correlation that high; Ouwehand 2021 shows scale/measure differences.

claim: Lab-to-field validity is thin: load ratings are validated mostly on university students in multimedia experiments (53 articles, N=7413), and human-LLM user studies using NASA-TLX measure the human, not the model. No study was found that gives an LLM a rating scale and validates it against behaviour (search was narrow). Update: field-like data exist (N=309 school students, HRV did not predict performance; effort rating beta +.309, load rating beta -.326) and a knowledge boundary (two-factor structure at low prior knowledge, three at high). The 'lab correlations did not hold outside the lab' claim is a mixed vote count in Skulmowski and Rey 2017, not a measured gap.
agent_test: Ask the agent to rate difficulty on a 9-point scale before solving and check against correctness (GAP 1).

claim: Relative condition efficiency (z performance minus z effort, over root two) combines accuracy and cost in one number but depends on the effort scale and a reference population. Formula recorded from the literature, paper not opened.
agent_test: Use accuracy per token (z accuracy minus z tokens) as the one efficiency number in every agent test.

claim: Physiology claims rest on counts of significance, not effect sizes: cardiac measures respond to workload (abstract only); the eye-tracking index did not separate groups in Korbach 2018 while Zu 2020 reports success; usability reviews mostly use performance (19%), NASA-TLX (12%), fixations (11%).
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM directly; logit entropy or attention entropy is the untested analogue (ICE pilot: attention entropy 4.44 to 5.04 over complexity levels).

claim: Item-level token count predicts error: within the same question, longer reasoning goes with lower accuracy (10 models, conditional correlation; o1-mini -3.16, o3-mini medium -1.96, o3-mini high -0.81 accuracy points per +1000 reasoning tokens). The slope shrinks with model capability, and the failed-step fraction predicts better than length.
agent_test: Log tokens and abandoned-branch share per item; fit error on tokens within item set; set a re-plan trigger at a per-model threshold.
audit_note: Feng et al. (ten LRMs, conditional within-question correlation, failed-step fraction beats length) and Ballon et al. (-3.16/-1.96/-0.81 per 1000 tokens, smaller for more proficient models) verified; slip: the three slope numbers come from Ballon's 3 models controlling for difficulty level, not from the 10-model Feng study.

claim: A model-internal pre-generation signal tracks model-specific difficulty better than length (Spearman .64 vs .27 for Qwen2.5-Math; .58 down to .40 for GPT-OSS-20B as reasoning rises) and supports routing at about 70% lower cost, but it weakens with reasoning effort and generalises poorly to math. Needs hidden states.
agent_test: Not available to a text-only scaffold; use output-side proxies (token share, branch failure, answer instability).

claim: Verbalised confidence given before solving is a weak and model-dependent predictor of correctness: frontier-model verbal AUROC .50 to .77 pre-solve vs .61 to .79 post-solve; post-solve is better. No study tests a 1 to 9 difficulty or effort rating before solving.
agent_test: Run the in-house test: pre-solve 1 to 9 rating vs correctness and tokens, per model; keep only if AUROC clearly above the token baseline.

claim: The TLX needs no weighting step for our purpose: the manual's own account says per-condition weights added only slight sensitivity, and the scale was cut from nine to six subscales for practicality. No reliability coefficient is in the manual; Hart and Staveland 1988 and DeLeeuw and Mayer 2008 numbers remain unrecovered.
agent_test: Use one raw number, not six subscales plus pairwise weights.

claim: Rating-scale format validity depends on task difficulty: on the same problems, pictorial scales tracked performance better for simple items and numeric scales (9-point, VAS) for complex items (N=46; accuracy .95 simple vs .51 complex).
agent_test: If the agent rates itself, use a numeric scale on hard items.
